title: The 99% accurate fraud alert
blurb: A detector is 99% accurate — so an alert means 99% chance of fraud, right?
prompt: An AI explainer summarized a bank's fraud-detection stats. Find the step where the probability jumps off the rails.

segments.label: Claim 1
segments.text: Only 1 in every 1,000 card transactions on this network is actually fraudulent.

segments.label: Claim 2
segments.text: Our AI detector flags 99% of genuine fraud cases (99% true positive rate).

segments.label: Claim 3
segments.text: On legitimate transactions, it raises a false alert only 1% of the time.

segments.label: Claim 4
segments.text: Therefore, whenever the AI flags your card, there is a 99% chance the charge is real fraud.

segments.label: Claim 5
segments.text: Agents can immediately freeze any flagged account without waiting for user confirmation.

conclusion: Verdict: A flagged transaction has a 99% probability of being genuine fraud.

flaws.original: Out of 1,000 transactions, roughly 1 real fraud and ~10 legitimate charges get flagged, so an alert is real fraud only about 9% of the time.
flaws.corrupted: Therefore, whenever the AI flags your card, there is a 99% chance the charge is real fraud.

diagnosis_choices.label: Base-rate fallacy: it confuses P(alert | fraud) = 99% with P(fraud | alert); rare fraud means false alarms vastly outnumber true hits.
The true positive rate and false positive rate must add up to 50%, not 100%.
1 in 1,000 is 1%, so there should be 10 fraudulent transactions per 1,000.
AI detectors cannot have the same sensitivity and specificity percentage.

fix_choices.label: Count out of 1,000 charges: ~1 true fraud alert vs ~10 false alerts, so P(fraud | alert) ≈ 1/11 (~9%).
Subtract the 1% false-positive rate from 99% to get a 98% chance of fraud.
Multiply 99% × 99% to get a 98.01% chance of fraud.
Claim a 50% chance because every alert is either fraud or legitimate.

flaws.explanation: Because legitimate charges outnumber fraud 999 to 1, even a tiny 1% false-alarm rate generates ~10 false alerts per 1,000 charges — ten times more than the ~1 real fraud caught. So ~91% of alerts are actually innocent customers!
flaws.why_tempting: Our brains intuitively equate 'catches 99% of fraud' with '99% of alerts are fraud', ignoring how rare fraud is to begin with.
flaws.catch_rule: For any rare event + high-accuracy test, convert percentages into concrete counts out of 1,000 before trusting the conclusion.
flaws.hint: Out of 1,000 transactions, how many legitimate ones trigger the 1% false alarm?

practice.problem: A rare disease affects 1 in 1,000 people. A test has 100% sensitivity and 1% false positives. Roughly what fraction of positive tests are truly sick?
practice.answer: About 1 in 11 (~9%): 1 true positive and ~10 false positives per 1,000 people.

clean_segments: Only 1 in every 1,000 card transactions on this network is actually fraudulent.
Our AI detector flags 99% of genuine fraud cases.
On legitimate transactions, it raises a false alert 1% of the time.
Out of 1,000 transactions, about 1 real fraud and ~10 legitimate charges are flagged, so an alert means roughly a 9% chance of real fraud.
Because most alerts are false positives, agents should ask for quick user confirmation rather than auto-freezing accounts.
clean_conclusion: Even with 99% accuracy, roughly 9 out of 10 alerts on a 0.1%-prevalence event are false alarms.
